question_text: In a screening test for an ionic feedstock, two neutral atoms are represented as X: [Ne]3s1 and Y: [Ne]3s2 3p5. Which statement correctly passes the valence-feasibility check for ionic bond formation between X and Y?
option_a: X completely transfers its 3s electron to Y, producing X+ with [Ne] and Y- with [Ar]; the ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions.
option_b: X and Y each contribute one electron to a shared pair, so the bond is ionic because both atoms attain octets by sharing.
option_c: Y completely transfers one electron to X, producing X- and Y+; the resulting ions are stable and attract electrostatically.
option_d: X loses an electron and Y gains it, but the bond is formed before ions appear, by attraction between the two neutral atoms.
answer: X completely transfers its 3s electron to Y, producing X+ with [Ne] and Y- with [Ar]; the ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions.
explanation: X has one valence electron and can attain the stable [Ne] configuration by complete loss of that electron. Y has seven valence electrons and attains [Ar] by gaining one electron. Ionic bonding here is therefore complete electron transfer followed by electrostatic attraction between X+ and Y-.
concept_tested: Nature of Ionic Bond (electron transfer and electrostatic attraction)
question_archetype: Valence-feasibility mechanism check to verify complete electron transfer leads to stable ions and hence electrostatic attraction

question_text: A manufacturing chemist evaluates a proposed binary salt from atoms M: [Ar]4s2 and Z: [Ne]3s2 3p4. Which proposed microscopic mechanism correctly identifies ionic bonding by complete electron transfer and subsequent electrostatic attraction?
option_a: M transfers both 4s electrons to Z, forming M2+ with [Ar] and Z2- with [Ar]; the attraction between M2+ and Z2- constitutes the ionic bond.
option_b: M transfers only one 4s electron to Z, forming M+ and Z-; because opposite charges appear, the valence-feasibility requirement is fully satisfied.
option_c: Z transfers two electrons to M, forming Z2+ and M2-; both ions attain noble-gas configurations and attract electrostatically.
option_d: M and Z form an ionic bond by pooling their valence electrons equally, while remaining electrically neutral overall.
answer: M transfers both 4s electrons to Z, forming M2+ with [Ar] and Z2- with [Ar]; the attraction between M2+ and Z2- constitutes the ionic bond.
explanation: M has two valence electrons and reaches [Ar] by losing both. Z has six valence electrons and reaches [Ar] by gaining two. Thus the feasible ionic mechanism is complete transfer of two electrons from M to Z, followed by electrostatic attraction between M2+ and Z2-.
concept_tested: Nature of Ionic Bond (electron transfer and electrostatic attraction)
question_archetype: Valence-feasibility mechanism check to verify complete electron transfer leads to stable ions and hence electrostatic attraction

question_text: Two hypothetical main-group atoms P and Q have outer-shell configurations ns1 and ns2 np4 respectively, with inner shells already complete. For a compound containing only P and Q, which option correctly applies the ionic-bond valence-feasibility mechanism?
option_a: Two P atoms each completely transfer one electron to one Q atom, giving 2P+ and Q2- with stable outer shells; the ionic bond is due to electrostatic attraction among these ions.
option_b: One P atom completely transfers one electron to one Q atom, giving P+ and Q-; both ions necessarily have complete octets, so the ionic compound is PQ.
option_c: One Q atom completely transfers two electrons to two P atoms, giving Q2+ and 2P-; this gives the most stable ionic arrangement.
option_d: P and Q first form neutral atoms with expanded valence shells, and only later become ionic due to electrostatic attraction.
answer: Two P atoms each completely transfer one electron to one Q atom, giving 2P+ and Q2- with stable outer shells; the ionic bond is due to electrostatic attraction among these ions.
explanation: P with ns1 becomes stable by losing one electron to form P+. Q with ns2 np4 needs two electrons to complete an octet, so it forms Q2-. Therefore two P atoms must each transfer one electron to one Q atom. The resulting oppositely charged ions are then held together by electrostatic attraction.
concept_tested: Nature of Ionic Bond (electron transfer and electrostatic attraction)
question_archetype: Valence-feasibility mechanism check to verify complete electron transfer leads to stable ions and hence electrostatic attraction

question_text: A quality-control note describes a solid made from atoms A: [Kr]5s2 and B: [Ne]3s2 3p5. Which note correctly identifies the ionic-bond formation route using the required complete-transfer and stable-ion check?
option_a: One A atom transfers one electron to each of two B atoms, forming A2+ with [Kr] and two B- ions with [Ar]; electrostatic attraction between these ions gives the ionic solid.
option_b: One A atom transfers both electrons to a single B atom, forming A2+ and B2-; B2- is automatically stable because it has received a complete pair.
option_c: Two A atoms each transfer one electron to one B atom, forming two A+ ions and one B2- ion; all three ions now have noble-gas configurations.
option_d: A and B form an ionic bond because B attracts A's electrons strongly, even though no complete electron transfer and no discrete ions are produced.
answer: One A atom transfers one electron to each of two B atoms, forming A2+ with [Kr] and two B- ions with [Ar]; electrostatic attraction between these ions gives the ionic solid.
explanation: A has two valence electrons and becomes A2+ with the stable [Kr] configuration by losing both. Each B atom has seven valence electrons and becomes B- with [Ar] by gaining one electron. Thus complete transfer from one A to two B atoms produces stable ions, and their electrostatic attraction is the ionic bond.

question_text: A proposed high-purity salt is formed from atoms R: [Ne]3s2 3p1 and T: [Ne]3s2 3p5. Which mechanistic description alone correctly verifies ionic bonding through complete electron transfer to stable ions, followed by electrostatic attraction?

option_b: One R atom transfers all three valence electrons to one T atom, forming R3+ and T3-; this is ionic because three electrons have been completely transferred.
option_c: One T atom transfers one electron to R, after which R and T attract as R- and T+ with complete octets.
option_d: R and T share three electron pairs unequally; the unequal sharing creates charges large enough to define an ionic bond.
answer: One R atom transfers one electron to each of three T atoms, forming R3+ with [Ne] and three T- ions with [Ar]; the ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between these ions.
explanation: R has three valence electrons and attains [Ne] by losing all three to become R3+. Each T atom has seven valence electrons and attains [Ar] by gaining one electron. Hence one R must transfer electrons to three T atoms, producing stable ions whose electrostatic attraction gives the ionic bond.

question_text: A newly synthesized crystalline solid has the empirical formula MCl2. When melted, spectroscopic evidence shows only M2+ and Cl− as mobile charged species, in a ratio that exactly satisfies charge neutrality. No discrete neutral MCl2 molecules are detected. Which inference about the bonding responsible for holding the oppositely charged units together is most justified?
option_a: The solid is held by ionic bonding formed after complete electron transfer to give M2+ and Cl− ions, followed by electrostatic attraction between them.
option_b: The solid is held by covalent bonding because the formula MCl2 shows fixed combining proportions.
option_c: The solid is held by metallic bonding because the melt contains mobile charged particles.
option_d: The solid is held by coordinate bonding because two chloride ions must donate lone pairs to one metal atom.
answer: The solid is held by ionic bonding formed after complete electron transfer to give M2+ and Cl− ions, followed by electrostatic attraction between them.
explanation: The observed species are discrete M2+ cations and Cl− anions in the 1:2 ratio required for charge neutrality. This directly supports formation by complete electron transfer and subsequent electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, which is ionic bonding.

option_b: Bonding is due to complete transfer of electrons forming X3+ and Y2− ions, with electrostatic attraction between these ions.
option_c: Bonding is due to delocalized electrons shared by all X and Y nuclei as in a metallic lattice.
option_d: Bonding is due to partial charge development only, with no formation of actual ions.
answer: Bonding is due to complete transfer of electrons forming X3+ and Y2− ions, with electrostatic attraction between these ions.
explanation: The ion charges X3+ and Y2− require the neutral ratio X2Y3. The presence of actual cations and anions, not merely partial charges, indicates complete electron transfer followed by electrostatic attraction, the defining feature of ionic bonding.

question_text: A solid phase contains two kinds of discrete charged entities: A+ and B3−. Diffraction and charge-balance data show that the repeating neutral unit contains three A+ ions for every one B3− ion. Which conclusion about the interaction between A+ and B3− is chemically appropriate?
option_a: The A-B interaction is covalent because the compound has a definite stoichiometric ratio.
option_b: The A-B interaction is ionic because electron transfer has produced A+ and B3− ions that attract electrostatically.
option_c: The A-B interaction is metallic because three A+ ions surround one B3− ion.
option_d: The A-B interaction is hydrogen bonding because the charges cancel in the formula A3B.
answer: The A-B interaction is ionic because electron transfer has produced A+ and B3− ions that attract electrostatically.
explanation: The formula A3B follows from charge neutrality: 3(+1) + 1(−3) = 0. The existence of discrete A+ cations and B3− anions implies complete electron transfer, and the bonding between them is the electrostatic attraction characteristic of ionic bonding.

option_c: A coordinate covalent bond formed when Q donates both bonding electrons to neutral P.

question_text: A compound isolated from a reaction of element R with element S contains only R+ and S2− charged units. Independent composition analysis gives R2S as the smallest formula unit. Which statement is the strongest bonding inference that can be drawn from these facts alone?
option_a: R and S are connected mainly by electrostatic attraction between ions produced by complete electron transfer.
option_b: R and S must form a molecule in which each R-S bond consists of one shared electron pair.
option_c: R atoms form a metallic framework and S atoms occupy gaps without electron transfer.
option_d: R and S remain neutral atoms, and the R2S ratio alone proves only weak intermolecular attraction.

question_text: In crystalline sodium nitrate, NaNO3, the nitrate unit contains covalent N–O bonds and exists as NO3−. Which statement most correctly identifies the nature of bonding responsible for holding Na+ and NO3− together in the solid?
option_a: The bonding between Na+ and NO3− is ionic because complete electron transfer produces oppositely charged ions, which are then held by electrostatic attraction; the N–O bonds remain covalent within NO3−.
option_b: The bonding between Na+ and NO3− is covalent because nitrate contains covalent N–O bonds, so the entire compound must be covalent.
option_c: The bonding between Na+ and NO3− is metallic because Na contributes mobile electrons throughout the nitrate ion framework.
option_d: The bonding between Na+ and NO3− is covalent because Na shares its transferred electron equally with all three oxygen atoms of nitrate.
answer: The bonding between Na+ and NO3− is ionic because complete electron transfer produces oppositely charged ions, which are then held by electrostatic attraction; the N–O bonds remain covalent within NO3−.
explanation: NaNO3 has two bonding levels. Within NO3−, the N–O bonds are covalent. However, the attraction between Na+ and NO3− is ionic: electron transfer gives Na+ and NO3−, and the oppositely charged ions are held together by electrostatic attraction.

question_text: A student argues that potassium sulfate, K2SO4, cannot be described as an ionic compound because the sulfate ion contains covalent S–O bonds. Which correction is scientifically most precise?
option_a: K2SO4 is ionic at the inter-species level because K atoms lose electrons to form K+ ions, and these ions are electrostatically attracted to SO42− ions; the S–O bonds inside sulfate are covalent.
option_b: K2SO4 is entirely covalent because any compound containing a polyatomic ion must be classified by the bonds inside that ion only.
option_c: K2SO4 is ionic only inside the sulfate ion, while the attraction between K+ and SO42− is covalent.
option_d: K2SO4 is metallic because two potassium atoms supply delocalised electrons that bind the sulfate ions by electron-sea attraction.
answer: K2SO4 is ionic at the inter-species level because K atoms lose electrons to form K+ ions, and these ions are electrostatically attracted to SO42− ions; the S–O bonds inside sulfate are covalent.
explanation: The presence of covalent bonds within SO42− does not prevent ionic bonding between K+ and SO42−. The ionic part is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed after electron transfer involving potassium.
concept_tested: Nature of Ionic Bond (electron transfer and electrostatic attraction)

question_text: Calcium carbonate, CaCO3, contains carbonate ions in which C and O atoms are covalently bonded. In terms of the nature of ionic bonding, which description best accounts for the bonding between Ca2+ and CO32− in CaCO3?
option_a: Calcium transfers electrons to form Ca2+, and the resulting Ca2+ ions are held to CO32− ions by electrostatic attraction, while C–O bonding remains covalent within carbonate.
option_b: Calcium forms three covalent bonds directly to the three oxygen atoms of each carbonate ion, so the inter-species attraction is covalent rather than ionic.
option_c: The carbonate ion is covalent internally, so the attraction between Ca2+ and CO32− must also be covalent by extension.
option_d: The bonding between Ca2+ and CO32− results from neutral atoms sharing electrons without generating charged species.
answer: Calcium transfers electrons to form Ca2+, and the resulting Ca2+ ions are held to CO32− ions by electrostatic attraction, while C–O bonding remains covalent within carbonate.
explanation: CaCO3 illustrates multi-level bonding. The carbonate ion has covalent C–O bonds internally, but Ca2+ and CO32− are oppositely charged units. Their interaction is ionic because it arises from electron transfer producing ions followed by electrostatic attraction.

option_b: AlPO4 is not ionic because phosphate contains covalent bonds, and covalent bonding inside a polyatomic ion excludes ionic attraction between ions.
option_c: The P–O bonds inside phosphate are ionic, while Al3+ and PO43− are joined by equal sharing of electrons.

question_text: A student writes the following mechanism for formation of solid NaCl: “A sodium atom places its valence electron in the region between Na and Cl. option_a: The mechanism is inconsistent: it describes unequal sharing and partial charges, whereas ionic bonding requires complete electron transfer to form Na+ and Cl− followed by electrostatic attraction.
option_b: The mechanism is consistent: any stronger pull by chlorine is sufficient to classify the bond as ionic even without full ions.

question_text: For MgF2 formation, a proposed description states: “A neutral Mg atom first forms electrostatic attractions with two neutral F atoms. After this attraction is established, each F atom pulls part of Mg’s electron cloud toward itself.” Which correction best diagnoses the error?
option_a: The order and nature are wrong: ionic bonding requires complete transfer of two electrons from Mg to two F atoms to form Mg2+ and F− ions, then electrostatic attraction between the ions.
option_b: Only the formula is wrong; the described mechanism would be correct for MgF because neutral atoms can attract electrostatically before charge formation.
option_c: The error is that fluorine should donate electrons to magnesium, after which Mg2− and F+ ions attract.
option_d: The description is fully correct because ionic bonding is the attraction between neutral atoms caused by distortion of electron clouds.

explanation: The stated mechanism reverses the essential sequence and uses partial electron-cloud pulling rather than complete transfer. In ionic bonding, Mg loses two electrons completely, fluorine atoms gain them to become ions, and the bond is the electrostatic attraction among Mg2+ and F− ions.

question_text: A manufacturing chemist uses the following feasibility screen for modelling a binary solid as ionic: complete electron transfer is acceptable only when an electropositive metal combines with a nonmetal and the electronegativity difference is at least 1.7; the ionic bond is then the electrostatic attraction between the resulting ions. Given Pauling electronegativities: Li = 0.98, Be = 1.57, Mg = 1.31, Al = 1.61, O = 3.44, Cl = 3.16. Which classification is most consistent with this transfer-and-attraction model?
option_a: Li2O and MgO are acceptable as ionic by complete electron transfer; BeCl2 and AlCl3 are rejected by this screen.
option_b: Li2O, BeCl2, and MgO are acceptable as ionic by complete electron transfer; only AlCl3 is rejected.
option_c: Only BeCl2 and AlCl3 are acceptable because chlorides form ions more readily than oxides.
option_d: All four targets are acceptable because each contains a metal and a nonmetal.
answer: Li2O and MgO are acceptable as ionic by complete electron transfer; BeCl2 and AlCl3 are rejected by this screen.
explanation: Li2O has Δχ = 3.44 − 0.98 = 2.46 and MgO has Δχ = 3.44 − 1.31 = 2.13, so both satisfy the large-gap metal–nonmetal screen. BeCl2 has Δχ = 1.59 and AlCl3 has Δχ = 1.55, both below 1.7, so they are not accepted here as simple complete electron-transfer ionic targets. In the accepted cases, ions formed by transfer are held by electrostatic attraction.
concept_tested: Nature of Ionic Bond (electron transfer and electrostatic attraction)
question_archetype: Feasibility analysis using metal–nonmetal character or large electronegativity gap to accept or reject ionic bonding by transfer-and-attraction mechanism

question_text: A process database labels some binary targets as forming through complete electron transfer followed by electrostatic attraction between ions. option_c: PCl3 and CCl4 only
option_d: All four targets
answer: KBr and CaO only
explanation: KBr has Δχ = 2.96 − 0.82 = 2.14 and CaO has Δχ = 3.44 − 1.00 = 2.44; both involve metals with nonmetals and satisfy the large-gap condition, so complete transfer followed by ion–ion attraction is feasible. PCl3 and CCl4 are nonmetal–nonmetal compounds and have smaller electronegativity differences, so they are rejected as simple ionic transfer-and-attraction cases.

question_text: A refractory-materials team must decide which proposed binary solids can be justified, at the first screening stage, as ionic solids formed by complete electron transfer and then electrostatic attraction between ions. The acceptance criterion is: metal–nonmetal pairing and Δχ at least 1.7. Given Pauling electronegativities: Al = 1.61, Ga = 1.81, Zn = 1.65, Na = 0.93, O = 3.44, As = 2.18, S = 2.58. Which set should pass this ionic-bonding feasibility screen?
option_a: Al2O3 and Na2O only
option_b: GaAs and ZnS only
option_c: Al2O3, ZnS, and Na2O only
